content: Vaginitis, specifically vulvovaginitis, is a prevalent condition that prompts many women to seek medical attention. It accounts for over 10% of visits to healthcare providers specializing in women’s health. This condition is characterized by symptoms such as itching, irritation, burning, and abnormal vaginal discharge. The three most common causes of vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age are bacterial vaginosis, Candida vulvovaginitis, and trichomoniasis. Patients with vulvovaginitis typically present with symptoms including vaginal discharge, itching, and dysuria (painful urination). Accurate diagnosis of vulvovaginitis requires a thorough history of the patient’s symptoms and sexual history. This information is critical for identifying the underlying cause. A physical examination should include an assessment of the external genitalia and a speculum examination. These evaluations should document the characteristics of the vaginal discharge, the presence of any vulvar or labial lesions, foreign bodies, cervical inflammation, cervical lesions, and any cervical motion or adnexal tenderness during a bimanual examination. It is essential to rule out pelvic inflammatory disease and cervical lesions as potential causes of vaginal discharge. Initial diagnostic tests include measuring vaginal pH and performing a wet mount examination of a vaginal smear. These tests help differentiate between the common etiologies of vulvovaginitis. Treatment involves targeted medical therapy to address the specific causative pathogen. Additionally, patients should receive counseling on proper hygiene, voiding techniques, and safe sexual practices. The prognosis for vulvovaginitis is generally favorable, although a small percentage of patients may experience recurrent episodes.
